title: Modal particles II: the attitude words
title_target: Det är väl en stor familj då.
goal: Hear and use the small unstressed words — *ju, väl, nog, då, alltså* and the younger *typ, liksom, asså, ba* — that tell the listener what you assume, expect or feel.
bekal: you can tell *ju* (we both know), *väl* (I assume, right?) and *nog* (I think, probably) apart
you can use *då* and *alltså* to push, sum up or react in a conversation
you can understand *typ*, *liksom*, *asså* and *ba* in young people's speech, including *ba* as "was like"
wave: Go back to Svenska 102, Unit 19: read the dialogue again and, for every *ju*, *väl* and *nog* you find, say the sentence once without the particle — then tell yourself in English what attitude went missing.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Pappas sextioårsdag
dialogs.intro: Lars is turning sixty, and in Sweden a round birthday is a big event. Elin and Dian are planning what to give him over breakfast in the flat.

lines.text: Du kommer väl på pappas sextioårsdag på lördag?

lines.literal: you come surely on dad's sixty-year-day on Saturday?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ja, det har jag ju lovat. Men vad ska jag ge honom?
lines.id: Yes, I promised, didn't I? But what should I give him?
lines.literal: yes, that have I as-you-know promised. but what shall I give him?

lines.text: Han vill nog inte ha något. Det säger han i alla fall.

lines.text: Vänta, hon är på jobbet. Hon svarar nog inte förrän efter fem.

lines.text: Okej. Alltså: jag köper boken, och du kollar med din mamma i kväll.

lines.text: Precis. Och klä dig inte för fint, det är ju bara familjen.

lines.id: Only family? There are thirty of you!
lines.literal: only family-the? you are as-you-know thirty persons!

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Ja, ja. Det är väl en stor familj då.
lines.id: Yeah, yeah. I guess it's a big family, then.
lines.literal: yes, yes. it is surely a big family then.

notes: **Du kommer väl…?** — *väl* (**vehl**) turns a statement into a request for confirmation: "you're coming, aren't you?", "surely you're coming?". It works like an English tag question, but sits inside the sentence. In a negative sentence it expresses a slight worry: *hon har väl inte redan köpt en?* (she hasn't already bought one, has she?).

**Det har jag ju lovat** — *ju* (**yü**) means "as you know, as we both know, after all". It appeals to shared knowledge and makes a statement sound self-evident. In Dian's last line, *Ni är ju trettio personer!*, it carries surprise at something obvious: "but there are thirty of you!" English often does this with stress or with "you know", "after all", "remember".

**Han vill nog inte…** — *nog* (**noog**) marks your own estimate: "probably, I think, I'd guess". It is softer than *säkert* and more personal than *förmodligen*. With strong stress, it can also mean "surely, sure enough": *Det ordnar sig NOG* (it'll work out, don't worry).

**Kom igen då** — *då* after a command or question adds urgency, impatience or encouragement: *Kom igen då!* (come on, then!), *Vad gör vi då?* (so what do we do?). At the end of Elin's last line, *Det är väl en stor familj då*, it shows resigned acceptance: "well, then I suppose it's a big family".

**Alltså** (**AHLT-soh**) — "so, in other words", used to sum up or draw a conclusion. In speech it often starts a reaction or a clarification: *Alltså, jag menar…* (I mean…). Fast and casual, it shrinks to **asså**, which you will hear from Jonas in the next dialogue.

**Sextioårsdag** (**SEKS-ti-ohsh-dahg**) — Swedes celebrate *jämna år* (round birthdays: 30, 40, 50, 60…) far more than other birthdays, often with a big party, speeches and a notice in the local paper. **I alla fall** ("anyway, at least") and **inte förrän** ("not until") are worth learning as fixed phrases.

grammars.title: The four classic attitude particles
body: These words are almost impossible to translate one-to-one, and they never carry the stress of the sentence. They sit in the sentence-adverb slot (Unit 1), right after the finite verb in a main clause: *Han kommer **ju** i morgon.* Leaving them out never makes a sentence wrong, but it can make you sound blunt.

head: Particle
What it signals
Rough English
Example
rows: you know, after all, of course
Det är ju lördag i morgon.
Det blir nog regn i kväll.
so, in other words, I mean

after: Particles combine, usually in the order **ju – väl/nog – inte**: *Han har **ju inte** ringt*, *Du har **väl inte** glömt?*, *Hon kommer **nog inte**.*
Unlike *ju*, *väl* and *nog*, the particle **då** usually goes at the **end** of a question or command. Inside a statement, *då* is just the ordinary time word "then": *Då köper jag en bok.*
With full stress, some of these become ordinary words: *Det gick VÄL* (it went well), *Det är NOG nu!* (that's enough now!).

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Jonas berättar om spelningen
dialogs.intro: Later that day Jonas comes home from a weekend of gigs with his band. He is twenty-three, and his Swedish sounds noticeably different from his sister's.

lines.text: Hur gick spelningen i går?
lines.id: How did the gig go yesterday?

lines.speaker: Jonas:
lines.text: Asså, det var typ det bästa vi har gjort. Folk ba dansade från första låten.
lines.id: I mean, it was like the best thing we've ever done. People were just dancing from the first song.
lines.literal: so, it was type the best we have done. people just danced from first song-the.

notes: **Asså** (**AHS-soh**) — the spoken form of *alltså*. At the start of a sentence it works like English "I mean", "well", "honestly": it buys time and announces that an opinion or an explanation is coming. *Nej men asså…* is a typical reaction when someone has said something you find a bit unfair.

**Typ** (**tüp**) — originally a noun (*en typ*, a type), now the Swedish equivalent of filler "like". It approximates numbers (*typ hundra* = about a hundred), hedges a description (*typ det bästa* = kind of the best) and fills pauses. Older speakers find it irritating; younger speakers barely notice it.

**Ba** (**bah**) — short for *bara* (just, only). Jonas uses it in two ways: *folk ba dansade* (people just danced) and, most typically, as a quotation marker: *jag ba: ”Vad gör du?”* = "I was like: 'What are you doing?'". This quotative *ba* is the closest Swedish has come to English "I was like".

**Liksom** (**LEEK-som**) — an older filler meaning "sort of, kind of, like". It softens a word (*liksom proppfull*) or keeps a sentence going. It belongs to all generations, which is why Elin would use *liksom* but not *typ*.

**Pers** (**pesh**) is slang for *personer*, used with numbers: *tio pers*, *hundra pers*. **Proppfull** (**PROP-fül**) means packed, crammed, from *en propp* (a plug). **En spelning** (**SPEHL-ning**) is a gig, **en lokal** (**loo-KAHL**) a venue or premises — a false friend, not "a local".

**Det var meningen** — "that was the idea, that was on purpose". *Meningen* here is "the intention", not "the sentence". The negative, *det var inte meningen*, is the standard way to say "I didn't mean to" — learn it, you will need it.

grammars.title: Like, like, like: four jobs for small words
body: Young Swedes' fillers do the same four jobs as English "like". Knowing which job a word is doing makes fast speech much easier to follow, even if you choose not to use the words yourself.
after: These words belong to relaxed speech and to chat messages. Use them sparingly with friends if you like, but keep them out of emails, seminars and job interviews. Unit 14 looks at register and slang more broadly.
*Liksom* and *alltså* are accepted in the speech of all ages; *typ*, *asså* and *ba* still mark the speaker as young or informal.

blocks.text: The best way to feel the particles is to keep a sentence constant and change only the small word. Read each line aloud with a natural, unstressed particle and notice how the speaker's relationship to the listener changes.

What the speaker is doing
English
rows: reminding you of what you know
So is he coming tomorrow, then?

blocks.text: Particles also appear in subordinate clauses, before the verb like every other sentence adverb: *Vi lagar inte fisk eftersom han **ju** inte gillar det.* Here *ju* reminds the listener that they already know the reason.

blocks.title: Pitfalls
items: Don't stress the particle: *det är JU lördag* sounds odd. The stress goes on the content word: *det är ju LÖRdag*.
*Ju* with something the listener can't know sounds presumptuous: *Jag har ju en bror i Malmö* to a stranger implies they should have known.
*Väl* in a statement can sound uncertain or reluctant: *Det är väl okej* = I suppose it's OK (not enthusiastic).

blocks.text: Particles assume a shared moment between speaker and listener, so most of them disappear in formal writing. When you turn spoken Swedish into a report, an application or a formal email, swap them for neutral equivalents.

Note that **alltså** survives in formal writing in its original sense, "consequently, thus": *Budgeten räcker alltså inte.* It is only the filler use (*Alltså, jag menar…*) that belongs to speech. In friendly emails and text messages, *ju* and *väl* are perfectly fine and make you sound warm rather than stiff.
